cards.front: State the Liverpool fieldwork enquiry question.
back: How far does environmental quality change across Liverpool town centre?

cards.front: State the River Alyn fieldwork enquiry question.
back: How do river characteristics change downstream along the River Alyn?

cards.front: Which sampling method collected data at regular points along a route?
back: Systematic sampling.

cards.front: Name one River Alyn characteristic that was measured.
back: Channel width.

cards.front: Name one indicator used in Liverpool's environmental-quality survey.
back: Litter.

cards.front: What is reliability?
back: Whether repeating a method gives similar results.

cards.front: Give two types of data collected in Liverpool.
back: Environmental-quality scores.
Pedestrian counts.

cards.front: Explain why pedestrian counts were completed for a set time.
back: A consistent duration makes results from different sites comparable.
It avoids a site appearing busier simply because it was observed for longer.

cards.front: Give two reported River Alyn downstream changes.
back: The channel generally became wider and deeper.
Bedload became smaller and rounder.

cards.front: Explain why several depth readings are taken across a channel.
back: River beds are uneven, so one reading may be unrepresentative.
Several readings allow a mean depth to be calculated.

cards.front: Explain the difference between quantitative and qualitative data.
back: Quantitative data is numerical, such as a pedestrian count.
Qualitative data is descriptive, such as an annotated field sketch.

cards.front: Give one strength and one limitation of an environmental-quality survey.
back: Strength: it turns several observations into comparable site scores.
Limitation: scores may be subjective and vary between observers.

cards.front: Explain how the Liverpool environmental-quality data was collected.
back: At each site, factors including litter, graffiti, noise, traffic, building condition and attractiveness were assessed.
Each factor was given a score using the survey scale.
Scores were added to produce a total that could be compared between sites.

cards.front: Explain why field sketches and land-use maps were useful in Liverpool.
back: They recorded the location of shops, services and other buildings.
They showed the character and function of each site.
This helped relate environmental quality and pedestrian flow to land use.

cards.front: Explain why bedload may become smaller and rounder downstream.
back: Stones are transported for longer distances downstream.
They collide with each other and the river bed.
Attrition chips edges, making them smaller and rounder.

cards.front: Explain why River Alyn velocity tended to increase downstream.
back: Tributaries and runoff add water, increasing discharge.
The channel becomes larger and usually more efficient.
Proportionally less water is slowed by contact with the bed and banks.

cards.front: Explain the main conclusion from the Liverpool investigation.
back: Environmental quality varied across the sampled parts of the town centre.
Central shopping areas generally had the highest quality scores.
These areas also had high pedestrian flow and concentrated retail and services.
Quieter streets away from the centre generally had lower scores and fewer pedestrians.

cards.front: Explain the main conclusion from the River Alyn investigation.
back: Width and depth generally increased downstream.
Velocity also tended to increase as the channel became more efficient.
Bedload became smaller and rounder through transport and attrition.
The overall pattern matched river theory, although local conditions may have affected individual sites.

cards.front: Explain how the reliability of pedestrian-flow data could be improved.
back: Repeat counts at each site rather than relying on one result.
Use the same count duration and clear counting rules.
Repeat at comparable times or days to reduce temporary effects.
Calculate a mean so one unusual count has less influence.

cards.front: Explain how the River Alyn investigation could improve its bedload sample.
back: Use the same systematic selection rule at every site.
Measure a larger number of stones.
Use the same equipment and roundness chart consistently.
Calculate a mean size and compare the distribution rather than one stone.
